Consider a minimal API for retrieval-augmented language generation. The function `propose(value, version)` returns a candidate; the function `commit(candidate)` checks its version and publishes it only when that version matches the current configuration. The identifier `commit` is part of the example API, not an instruction to execute a command. The retriever may call `propose` repeatedly while searching for an acceptable result. The generator sees only candidates that pass the final check, so the number of proposals can exceed the number of published results.

Suppose the configuration changes between proposal and publication. A comparison against the old version would admit an obsolete candidate. The implementation instead compares against the version stored at publication time. A failed comparison discards the candidate and leaves the previously published result available. It does not clear the visible result merely to make the state appear fresh. This behavior is especially relevant when the user requests a replacement and the replacement later fails.

The regression test records the values of `proposal_count`, `commit_count`, and `visible_version`. It first publishes one valid candidate, then attempts to publish a stale candidate. The first counter increases on both attempts, the second increases only on the successful publication, and the third continues to identify the valid result. Counting the stale candidate as a successful commit would make the summary disagree with the visible state. The original documents are retained so that the failed attempt can be reproduced under the same configuration.

We compare two systems for retrieval-augmented language generation. The first combines an adaptive retriever with a fixed generator; the second keeps both components fixed. To avoid ambiguity, this section calls them the adaptive system and the fixed system. A third configuration, introduced only in the final ablation, disables the retriever entirely. It is not the same as the fixed system. All three configurations receive identical documents, but only the first two are included in the main comparison. References to "both systems" below therefore exclude the third configuration.

The primary endpoint is answer accuracy. The secondary endpoint is retrieval recall. These endpoints are reported separately because improving one need not improve the other. We define an improvement relative to the fixed system under the same workload and measurement procedure. A result obtained under a different workload is described as a separate experiment, even if its numerical value happens to be better. The primary table contains five independently initialized runs for each system. Repeated observations within a run are used to estimate that run's endpoint; they are not counted as additional independent runs.

The development workload contains answerable questions, whereas the stress workload includes unanswerable questions. The stress workload is constructed before inspecting the final outputs. It remains unchanged throughout the comparison. Neither system may use the stress outputs to select a checkpoint or adjust a threshold. When the adaptive system updates its internal state during inference, those updates are part of the evaluated method. They do not authorize an experimenter to alter the externally specified threshold after seeing a failure. This distinction matters because otherwise adaptation and retrospective tuning would be indistinguishable.

At the start of each run, both systems have empty application caches. The retriever may nevertheless reuse immutable preprocessing shared by all configurations. We measure this preprocessing separately and disclose it in the report. The first timed request begins only after preprocessing has finished. A second table includes the preprocessing cost, allowing readers to assess a one-shot use case. These two tables answer different questions. Their numbers must not be added together, because the second already includes the work described by the first. A cache hit inside the timed region is recorded explicitly.

The adaptive system performs better on the development workload in four of the five runs. In the remaining run, the difference is smaller than the measurement resolution. This observation does not establish that the adaptive system is universally superior. On the stress workload, it fails on two inputs that the fixed system handles successfully. Conversely, the fixed system fails on three inputs that the adaptive system handles successfully. We retain every failure in the denominator when reporting completion rates. Quality among completed outputs is also reported, but it is labeled as a conditional statistic.

Inspection of the failed cases suggests an important limitation: the generator may produce a fluent answer unsupported by retrieved evidence. The inspection identifies a plausible mechanism, not a proven causal explanation. To test that mechanism, a follow-up experiment would need to vary the suspected factor while holding other factors constant. The present comparison does not do that. Its evidence supports a narrower statement: the observed failures are consistent with the proposed mechanism. Translating this statement as a demonstration of causality would materially strengthen the claim beyond the evidence supplied by the experiment.

Finally, the ablation without the retriever is evaluated on a small diagnostic subset. It helps determine whether that component contributes to the observed behavior, but it is not used to replace either main system in the headline comparison. The diagnostic subset is deliberately enriched for difficult cases and does not estimate their frequency in ordinary use. We therefore publish its results separately. The released configuration, dataset identifiers, and individual run records make the comparison reproducible; they do not guarantee that a different machine or workload will reproduce the same absolute timings.

A. Source identity. Verify the exact documents used by the archived experiment. A matching file name is insufficient when the content differs. Store both the retrieval location and a content fingerprint so that another investigator can distinguish renaming from modification.

State whether the problem concerns an incorrect relation, an omitted condition, or an unsupported addition. The possibility that the generator may produce a fluent answer unsupported by retrieved evidence should guide inspection without predetermining its conclusion.

A replication study revisits an earlier comparison of multi-view scene reconstruction. The original report evaluated a baseline and a modified system. The replication retains those names, but it introduces an additional implementation of the baseline on a different machine. This additional implementation is called the port. The port is intended to implement the same method as the baseline; it is not a third method with a new objective. Statements about the two methods refer to the baseline and the modified system, whereas statements about the three implementations also include the port.

The replication begins by checking whether the archived images can be recovered exactly. It compares content fingerprints before any measurement takes place. Two files have different names but identical contents, while one file has the original name but altered contents. The first pair is treated as the same input. The altered file is excluded from the matched comparison and listed separately. File names alone therefore do not determine whether an input belongs to the replicated experiment. This decision is made before examining the new outputs.

The baseline uses a fixed camera estimator followed by a fixed renderer. The modified system changes the first component but leaves the second component unchanged. The port uses a different low-level implementation of both components while preserving their specified behavior. If the port produces a different accepted output on a deterministic test, the investigators treat that difference as a compatibility issue. They do not immediately attribute it to the scientific method. The report records the implementation difference so that a later analysis can separate methodological effects from software defects.

For each implementation, the investigators measure reconstruction error and rendering speed. They avoid combining these measures into one number because the tradeoff depends on the intended use. A reader interested in occasional interactive use may value the first result differently from a reader processing a large collection overnight. The report supplies both measurements and the conditions under which they were obtained. It does not infer a universal preference from one workload. Measurements that were unavailable after a process failure remain explicitly missing in the archive.

The replication uses a matched design: each implementation receives the same input sequence within a pair of runs. The order of implementations alternates across pairs to reduce the influence of gradual background changes. There are four pairs, rather than four observations from a single uninterrupted run. Each pair starts from a documented cache state. The investigators report the difference within each pair before averaging those differences. They also show the range, because a small average can conceal substantial variation between pairs.

On ordinary inputs, the modified system improves the primary measurement in three pairs and worsens it slightly in one. On a separately frozen subset of difficult inputs, that pattern reverses. The subset contains more occluded views than the ordinary collection, so its aggregate result is not used as an estimate of everyday performance. The original collection contains mostly well-lit views. Neither fact makes the other evaluation invalid. They characterize different operating conditions, and the distinction between them must remain visible in the interpretation.

An inspection again finds that a visually smooth surface may still have incorrect depth. However, the available records cannot establish whether this issue caused every observed failure. Some failed runs also experienced a resource limit, and their partial outputs cannot be treated as complete evidence. The investigators preserve those outputs for diagnosis but exclude them from claims that require a completed response. They still count the failed runs in reliability statistics. This separation prevents a method from appearing more reliable merely because its difficult cases disappeared from the quality table.

The final conclusion is limited. The replication confirms that the archived comparison can be reconstructed and that the direction of the ordinary-workload effect is broadly consistent across the matched runs. It does not confirm identical absolute timing, universal superiority, or correctness on inputs outside the tested distribution. The port remains useful as a compatibility check, but its measurements are labeled with its own environment. Future revisions must keep the original records and create a new comparison instead of silently replacing the historical result.

Protocol for evaluating multi-view scene reconstruction:

1. Prepare the images. Record the configuration identifier and the order of the inputs before either system runs. Retain the original ordering in the archive, even when a randomized execution order is used during measurement.

Acceptance condition: every scheduled input has exactly one terminal record, all configuration identifiers are recoverable, and no missing observation is silently replaced. Passing this condition establishes that the experiment was recorded consistently. It does not establish that the evaluated method is correct on every possible input. The original inputs remain available for a later rerun.

A replication study revisits an earlier comparison of approximate vector search. The original report evaluated a baseline and a modified system. The replication retains those names, but it introduces an additional implementation of the baseline on a different machine. This additional implementation is called the port. The port is intended to implement the same method as the baseline; it is not a third method with a new objective. Statements about the two methods refer to the baseline and the modified system, whereas statements about the three implementations also include the port.

The replication begins by checking whether the archived vectors can be recovered exactly. It compares content fingerprints before any measurement takes place. Two files have different names but identical contents, while one file has the original name but altered contents. The first pair is treated as the same input. The altered file is excluded from the matched comparison and listed separately. File names alone therefore do not determine whether an input belongs to the replicated experiment. This decision is made before examining the new outputs.

The baseline uses a fixed coarse index followed by a fixed reranker. The modified system changes the first component but leaves the second component unchanged. The port uses a different low-level implementation of both components while preserving their specified behavior. If the port produces a different accepted output on a deterministic test, the investigators treat that difference as a compatibility issue. They do not immediately attribute it to the scientific method. The report records the implementation difference so that a later analysis can separate methodological effects from software defects.

For each implementation, the investigators measure recall at ten and query latency. They avoid combining these measures into one number because the tradeoff depends on the intended use. A reader interested in occasional interactive use may value the first result differently from a reader processing a large collection overnight. The report supplies both measurements and the conditions under which they were obtained. It does not infer a universal preference from one workload. Measurements that were unavailable after a process failure remain explicitly missing in the archive.

They also show the range, because a small average can conceal substantial variation between pairs.

We compare two systems for incremental static analysis. The first combines an adaptive parser with a fixed type checker; the second keeps both components fixed. To avoid ambiguity, this section calls them the adaptive system and the fixed system. A third configuration, introduced only in the final ablation, disables the parser entirely. It is not the same as the fixed system. All three configurations receive identical program modules, but only the first two are included in the main comparison. References to "both systems" below therefore exclude the third configuration.

The primary endpoint is diagnostic precision. The secondary endpoint is analysis time. These endpoints are reported separately because improving one need not improve the other. We define an improvement relative to the fixed system under the same workload and measurement procedure. A result obtained under a different workload is described as a separate experiment, even if its numerical value happens to be better. The primary table contains five independently initialized runs for each system. Repeated observations within a run are used to estimate that run's endpoint; they are not counted as additional independent runs.

The development workload contains well-typed programs, whereas the stress workload includes ill-typed programs. The stress workload is constructed before inspecting the final outputs. It remains unchanged throughout the comparison. Neither system may use the stress outputs to select a checkpoint or adjust a threshold. When the adaptive system updates its internal state during inference, those updates are part of the evaluated method. They do not authorize an experimenter to alter the externally specified threshold after seeing a failure. This distinction matters because otherwise adaptation and retrospective tuning would be indistinguishable.

At the start of each run, both systems have empty application caches. The parser may nevertheless reuse immutable preprocessing shared by all configurations. We measure this preprocessing separately and disclose it in the report. The first timed request begins only after preprocessing has finished. A second table includes the preprocessing cost, allowing readers to assess a one-shot use case. These two tables answer different questions. Their numbers must not be added together, because the second already includes the work described by the first. A cache hit inside the timed region is recorded explicitly.

The adaptive system performs better on the development workload in four of the five runs. In the remaining run, the difference is smaller than the measurement resolution. This observation does not establish that the adaptive system is universally superior. On the stress workload, it fails on two inputs that the fixed system handles successfully. Conversely, the fixed system fails on three inputs that the adaptive system handles successfully. We retain every failure in the denominator when reporting completion rates. Quality among completed outputs is also reported, but it is labeled as a conditional statistic.

Inspection of the failed cases suggests an important limitation: successful parsing does not establish that a program is type safe. The inspection identifies a plausible mechanism, not a proven causal explanation. To test that mechanism, a follow-up experiment would need to vary the suspected factor while holding other factors constant. The present comparison does not do that. Its evidence supports a narrower statement: the observed failures are consistent with the proposed mechanism. Translating this statement as a demonstration of causality would materially strengthen the claim beyond the evidence supplied by the experiment.

Finally, the ablation without the parser is evaluated on a small diagnostic subset. It helps determine whether that component contributes to the observed behavior, but it is not used to replace either main system in the headline comparison. The diagnostic subset is deliberately enriched for difficult cases and does not estimate their frequency in ordinary use. We therefore publish its results separately. The released configuration, dataset identifiers, and individual run records make the comparison reproducible; they do not guarantee that a different machine or workload will reproduce the same absolute timings.

The implementation instead compares against the version stored at publication time. A failed comparison discards the candidate and leaves the previously published result available. It does not clear the visible result merely to make the state appear fresh. This behavior is especially relevant when the user requests a replacement and the replacement later fails.

The regression test records the values of `proposal_count`, `commit_count`, and `visible_version`. It first publishes one valid candidate, then attempts to publish a stale candidate. The first counter increases on both attempts, the second increases only on the successful publication, and the third continues to identify the valid result. Counting the stale candidate as a successful commit would make the summary disagree with the visible state. We compare two systems for interactive visualization design. The first combines an adaptive selection controller with a fixed view renderer; the second keeps both components fixed. To avoid ambiguity, this section calls them the adaptive system and the fixed system. A third configuration, introduced only in the final ablation, disables the selection controller entirely. It is not the same as the fixed system. All three configurations receive identical visual marks, but only the first two are included in the main comparison. References to "both systems" below therefore exclude the third configuration.

The primary endpoint is task completion time. The secondary endpoint is error rate. These endpoints are reported separately because improving one need not improve the other. We define an improvement relative to the fixed system under the same workload and measurement procedure. A result obtained under a different workload is described as a separate experiment, even if its numerical value happens to be better. The primary table contains five independently initialized runs for each system. Repeated observations within a run are used to estimate that run's endpoint; they are not counted as additional independent runs.

The development workload contains first-time participants, whereas the stress workload includes experienced participants. The stress workload is constructed before inspecting the final outputs. It remains unchanged throughout the comparison. Neither system may use the stress outputs to select a checkpoint or adjust a threshold. When the adaptive system updates its internal state during inference, those updates are part of the evaluated method. They do not authorize an experimenter to alter the externally specified threshold after seeing a failure. This distinction matters because otherwise adaptation and retrospective tuning would be indistinguishable.

At the start of each run, both systems have empty application caches. The selection controller may nevertheless reuse immutable preprocessing shared by all configurations. We measure this preprocessing separately and disclose it in the report. The first timed request begins only after preprocessing has finished. A second table includes the preprocessing cost, allowing readers to assess a one-shot use case. These two tables answer different questions. Their numbers must not be added together, because the second already includes the work described by the first. A cache hit inside the timed region is recorded explicitly.

The adaptive system performs better on the development workload in four of the five runs. In the remaining run, the difference is smaller than the measurement resolution. This observation does not establish that the adaptive system is universally superior. On the stress workload, it fails on two inputs that the fixed system handles successfully. Conversely, the fixed system fails on three inputs that the adaptive system handles successfully. We retain every failure in the denominator when reporting completion rates. Quality among completed outputs is also reported, but it is labeled as a conditional statistic.

Inspection of the failed cases suggests an important limitation: a participant may finish quickly while misunderstanding the represented uncertainty. The inspection identifies a plausible mechanism, not a proven causal explanation. To test that mechanism, a follow-up experiment would need to vary the suspected factor while holding other factors constant. The present comparison does not do that. Its evidence supports a narrower statement: the observed failures are consistent with the proposed mechanism. Translating this statement as a demonstration of causality would materially strengthen the claim beyond the evidence supplied by the experiment.

Finally, the ablation without the selection controller is evaluated on a small diagnostic subset. It helps determine whether that component contributes to the observed behavior, but it is not used to replace either main system in the headline comparison. The diagnostic subset is deliberately enriched for difficult cases and does not estimate their frequency in ordinary use. We therefore publish its results separately. The released configuration, dataset identifiers, and individual run records make the comparison reproducible; they do not guarantee that a different machine or workload will reproduce the same absolute timings.

Statements about the two methods refer to the baseline and the modified system, whereas statements about the three implementations also include the port.

Two files have different names but identical contents, while one file has the original name but altered contents. The first pair is treated as the same input. The altered file is excluded from the matched comparison and listed separately. File names alone therefore do not determine whether an input belongs to the replicated experiment. This decision is made before examining the new outputs.

The baseline uses a fixed compactor followed by a fixed query estimator. The modified system changes the first component but leaves the second component unchanged. The port uses a different low-level implementation of both components while preserving their specified behavior. If the port produces a different accepted output on a deterministic test, the investigators treat that difference as a compatibility issue. They do not immediately attribute it to the scientific method. The report records the implementation difference so that a later analysis can separate methodological effects from software defects.

A reader interested in occasional interactive use may value the first result differently from a reader processing a large collection overnight. The report supplies both measurements and the conditions under which they were obtained. It does not infer a universal preference from one workload. Measurements that were unavailable after a process failure remain explicitly missing in the archive.

Each pair starts from a documented cache state. The investigators report the difference within each pair before averaging those differences. They also show the range, because a small average can conceal substantial variation between pairs.

The subset contains more adversarial streams than the ordinary collection, so its aggregate result is not used as an estimate of everyday performance. The original collection contains mostly uniform streams. Neither fact makes the other evaluation invalid. They characterize different operating conditions, and the distinction between them must remain visible in the interpretation.

An inspection again finds that a probabilistic rank guarantee is not a guarantee on the numerical distance between values. However, the available records cannot establish whether this issue caused every observed failure. Some failed runs also experienced a resource limit, and their partial outputs cannot be treated as complete evidence. The investigators preserve those outputs for diagnosis but exclude them from claims that require a completed response. They still count the failed runs in reliability statistics. This separation prevents a method from appearing more reliable merely because its difficult cases disappeared from the quality table.

The replication confirms that the archived comparison can be reconstructed and that the direction of the ordinary-workload effect is broadly consistent across the matched runs. It does not confirm identical absolute timing, universal superiority, or correctness on inputs outside the tested distribution. The port remains useful as a compatibility check, but its measurements are labeled with its own environment. Future revisions must keep the original records and create a new comparison instead of silently replacing the historical result.
